# Acetate

**Overview:** [[Acetate]] is the two-carbon short-chain fatty acid (CH₃COO⁻) and the most abundant [[Short-chain Fatty Acids|SCFA]] produced by gut fermentation. It is generated by anaerobic bacteria (notably [[Bifidobacterium]], *Bacteroides*, and acetogens) from dietary fiber and by host [[Acetyl-CoA]] metabolism.

**Production and Absorption:** Gut microbes convert carbohydrates to acetate, which is absorbed into portal blood and distributed systemically. Acetate can cross membranes as the protonated acid or via monocarboxylate transporters, reaching the liver, brain, and periphery.

**Physiological Function:** In the liver, acetate is activated to [[Acetyl-CoA]] and incorporated into lipids, cholesterol, and ketone bodies—linking the [[Gut Microbiome]] to host [[Lipid Metabolism|lipid/energy metabolism]]. It serves as a substrate for脂肪酸 synthesis and, in the brain, can be used by astrocytes for acetyl-CoA and neurotransmitter synthesis. Acetate also signals via G-protein-coupled receptors (free fatty acid receptors) to modulate inflammation and appetite.

**Immune and Metabolic Regulation:** Acetate exerts systemic anti-inflammatory effects, promotes T-regulatory cell function, and influences blood pressure and satiety. It is a key mediator by which the microbiome shapes metabolic and immune homeostasis, and it feeds the acetyl group pool used in [[Acetylation]] (including [[Histone Acetylation]]).

**Longevity Relevance:** SCFA profiles, including acetate, are altered in aging and are modulated by diet, [[Caloric Restriction]], and [[Nicotinamide Riboside|NAD+ precursors]]. Acetate sits at the intersection of microbial metabolism, [[Metabolism]], and epigenetic regulation.
